title_original: Planches Contact Festival 2026 : The Young Photographers’ Award
excerpt_original: Flore Prebay, Emeline Sauser, Juliette Pavy and Mathias Benguigui have been shortlisted for the 2026 Young Photographic Creation Prize at the Planches Contact festival in Deauville Cet article Planches Contact Festival 2026 : The Young Photographers’ Award est apparu en premier…

blocks.text: For the 17th edition of the Planches Contact Festival, Les Franciscaines in Deauville is presenting the work of four photographers selected for the Prix de la Jeune Création Photographique. During their residencies in Normandy, they developed close relationships with local residents, leaving traces in both memories and images.

Before taking photographs, they listened. Caregivers remain in the shadows, a life draws to a close, the last witnesses of the war pass away, and shipwrecks slowly corrode beneath the sea. During their residencies in Normandy, Flore Prebay, Emeline Sauser, Juliette Pavy and Mathias Benguigui gathered what time threatened to erase. Selected for the Prix de la Jeune Création Photographique, which supports emerging photographers aged 18 to 35, they are presenting their projects at Les Franciscaines in Deauville as part of the 17th Planches Contact Festival.
The time of a dream, “the space of a night”

“Step inside this little cabin of dreams,” invites Flore Prébay. Against sky-blue exhibition walls, reminiscent of a small corner of paradise, Les Présents , a photographic and artistic project devoted to caregivers, unfolds with remarkable lightness. Having herself become a caregiver while accompanying her mother at the end of her life, the artist wanted to pay tribute to those who support a loved one in their daily lives. “I met caregivers from the region and asked them a question: ‘If you had a moment entirely to yourself, what would your innermost dream be?’” she explains.

A hike, building a greenhouse, a simple moment of rest: these dreams take shape on sheets of paper with a captivating material quality, handmade by her uncle, a papermaking artist, and on fabrics that move as visitors pass by. Notebooks hang on the walls, containing the stories of the families Flore Prebay interviewed. This project has earned her an invitation to the InCadaqués festival.

In a different way, Emeline Sauser also accompanied someone approaching the end of his life. While pursuing a project in which she sought to spend a night in a stranger’s home, the photographer, with the help of a journalist from Ouest-France , placed a classified advertisement in the newspaper. Thibault responded: “I’ve been ill for 15 years, following several relapses after a bone marrow transplant. I’ve been told I have little time left, in the short or medium term at best. I have a sword of Damocles hanging over my head.”

“I was supposed to spend one night at his home. It turned into four months,” the photographer recalls. Alongside him and his friends, she captured the night, the roads and an urgent desire to live. The project takes the form of a heartfelt letter to Thibault, who has since passed away. Words are interspersed among the images. For this singularly poetic work, Emeline Sauser received the Jury Prize: a residency at Villa Pérochon.

Telling stories before it is too late is also central to Mathias Benguigui’s approach. For him, the camera is “a shovel used to uncover the wounds” buried in Normandy’s battlefields. “Last year, I lost a friend, Antoni Lallican, who was killed by a Russian drone in Ukraine. From that moment, I wanted to reflect on how to depict war, how it leaves traces in landscapes and in memory,” he explains.

He began exploring his own family history, investigating the landscapes of Normandy, recording the testimonies of the last survivors of the Second World War and collecting screenshots of images of bombings in Iran. Panser nos guerres is a “vast cloud of images engraved on paper, on copper, but also on plaster containing remnants of war gathered across the region,” the photographer explains.

Not far from this cloud of photographs, Juliette Pavy also examines what war has left behind in the region. With Les Eaux Noires , she dives among the shipwrecks scattered across the seabed off the Normandy coast. “These wrecks contain large quantities of fuel and ammunition cargoes that pollute the oceans,” the artist explains.

How can this invisible pollution be represented through images? She meets scientists from the Institut de la Corrosion in Brest and specialists at a pollution-control centre dealing with oil spills, before diving herself to depths of around thirty metres, approaching these ecological time bombs. The result is a photographic investigation into the urgency of taking action.
In Deauville, these stories are not simply there to be seen: they ask, in turn, to be heard.
